quickAnswer: Wellesley has the oldest median home of the 50 towns we serve (built 1954), the 2nd-highest home values, and its own municipal electric utility. That combination makes the rebate rules and careful sizing worth checking before any purchase.
body: ## The oldest median house in the 50 towns

Of the 50 towns we serve, Wellesley has the oldest median home. The Census Bureau's 2022 survey (ACS) dates the median Wellesley home to 1954. 3,255 of the town's 9,320 housing units (34.9%) date from 1939 or earlier, the 2nd-highest share, and 6,940 (74.5%) predate 1980, also 2nd. For comparison, the middle town has 16.6% built in 1939 or earlier. Another 2,251 homes (24.2%) date from 1940 to 1959.

Wikipedia says Wellesley's population grew by over 80 percent around the 1920s. The town was settled in the 1600s as part of Dedham, then belonged to Needham as West Needham. Residents voted to secede on October 23, 1880, and the legislature christened the town Wellesley on April 6, 1881, after the estate of local benefactor Horatio Hollis Hunnewell.

Older houses can have plaster walls, uneven insulation, additions built in different decades and boilers that have been replaced more than once. In the historic district on Cottage Street, most houses were built around the 1860s and are protected buildings under the town's historic commission, so visible changes to those buildings may come with extra rules.
## Worth a great deal, so sized carefully

The median owner-occupied home in Wellesley is worth $1,424,400, the 2nd-highest value of the 50 towns. A system sized from the old unit may be too large for a house that has since been insulated, or too small for an addition. Sizing from the house as it stands today, rather than from the old equipment, is the sensible starting point.
## Gas is the norm, oil and bottled gas are rare

Utility gas heats 6,379 occupied homes (71.2%), the 3rd-highest share among the 50 towns. Fuel oil heats 1,511 (16.9%), the 5th-lowest share of the 50, and bottled gas only 127 homes (1.4%), the 2nd-lowest. Electricity heats 855 homes (9.5%). An oil boiler is the exception here, and replacing one raises the question of whether to convert. A gas conversion needs a main on the street, a permit and an inspection. Detached houses make up 7,672 of the 9,320 units (82.3%), against 76.7% in the middle town, and renters hold 1,395 of the 8,956 occupied homes. The town covers 10.49 square miles in total area, bordered by Newton, Weston, Needham, Dover and Natick.
## The Wellesley Municipal Light Plant

Electricity comes from the Wellesley Municipal Light Plant, not an investor-owned utility. That changes the heat pump rules. Because the utility is municipal, the rebate path for a heat pump depends on how the house heats, and the rule is spelled out on the heat pump page. Wikipedia adds that the three colleges voluntarily pay a premium to buy wind-generated electricity, and that the EPA designated Wellesley a Green Power Community in 2012. Read the rule on the [heat pump page](/cities/wellesley/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).
## Rebuilt in the new century

Not everything is old. 1,544 homes (16.6%) date from 2000 or later and 974 (10.5%) from 2010 onward, the 15th-highest share, which makes them a visible minority beside the pre-war stock. Wikipedia lists several rebuilds: a pre-World War II high school replaced by a new one finished in 2012, a historic inn demolished in 2006 for condominiums, and the Linden Street strip-mall replaced by Linden Square. Town Meeting adopted the Massachusetts Stretch Building Code effective January 2012.

faq.q: Are Mass Save heat pump rebates available in Wellesley?
faq.a: It depends on how the house heats, because the electric utility here is municipal. Gas-heated homes are the ones Mass Save generally covers, and the Wellesley Municipal Light Plant has its own program for the rest. Terms change, so confirm them before buying equipment.

faq.q: Why does the age of Wellesley houses matter for a new system?
faq.a: The median home dates to 1954, and about a third of units are from 1939 or earlier. Older houses vary widely in insulation, ducts and piping, so equipment should be sized from the house. That is why we assess the heating load first.

faq.q: Is it common to heat with oil in Wellesley?
faq.a: No. Oil heats 16.9% of occupied homes, one of the lowest shares among the 50 towns, and gas heats 71.2%. Oil owners usually face a choice between replacing the boiler, converting to gas if a main is available, or adding a heat pump.

faq.q: How do Wellesley home values compare with the other towns?
faq.a: Very high. The median owner-occupied home is worth $1,424,400, the 2nd-highest among the 50 towns we serve, while the middle town sits at $579,150. Detached houses are 82.3% of units. At those values, sizing and installation quality are worth more attention than the lowest price on a quote, and a written estimate makes that comparison easy.

heating-installation-repair.quickAnswer: Gas heats most Wellesley homes, so a replacement is often a new gas boiler or furnace. The size and the piping start from the building, because radiators, plaster and additions can all shape them.
body: ## Replacing heat in houses that have been here a long time

With gas as the main fuel, a replacement is often a gas boiler or furnace that has reached the end of its life in an older house. Oil and bottled gas are uncommon here, so an oil system raises the question of whether to convert.
### Old houses, mixed systems

A house from the early twentieth century may have steam or hot-water radiators, a later addition on a separate zone and a bathroom heated by something else. The whole house should be mapped, what feeds what, before a replacement is chosen. Steam systems need careful piping and a proper pressure test, and a new boiler should be sized to the radiators and the house as they are today.
### What we look at

- The load of the house today, after any insulation or window work.
- Radiators, baseboard and ducts, and whether they can be reused.
- Venting, gas piping and combustion air.
- Room for the new equipment and a clear path to get the old one out.
### Permits

A gas boiler or furnace swap goes through a permit and then an inspection, and in Massachusetts the permit must be pulled by a licensed plumber or gas fitter. Ask the town's building department about local requirements. Historic houses may have additional rules for work that affects the exterior, such as new vents or outdoor equipment.
### Oil to gas

If an oil system fails, we explain what a conversion involves: a gas line to the house, a new appliance, removing or properly closing the oil tank, and the permit and inspection. We also compare a heat pump, since the municipal utility's program can change the math.

### Larger buildings
Multifamily housing here is modest: 790 homes (8.5%) are in buildings of five or more units, with 271 in two-unit buildings and 253 in buildings of three or four. A shared plant, or one boiler per unit, changes who has to be reached before work.
### Rental properties

Renters make up 15.6% of Wellesley households. The sanitary code sets 68 F by day and 64 F overnight in the heating season, and unless the lease says otherwise the landlord pays for heat. A failed rental boiler is an emergency at any hour, and we take those calls day or night.
Call (508) 786-8755 for emergencies. The [maintenance page](/cities/wellesley/hvac-maintenance-tune-ups) covers how annual checks reduce the chance of a failure.

faq.q: Can I reuse the radiators when I replace a Wellesley boiler?
faq.a: Usually yes. Many cast-iron radiators last for decades. We check them and the piping, then size the new boiler for the actual load of the house, which may be smaller than the old boiler.

faq.q: Should I convert from oil to gas?
faq.a: It depends on whether a main serves your street and the cost to connect. Gas heats 71.2% of homes, yet that does not put a main on every street. We also price a heat pump so you can compare.

faq.q: What changes when a Wellesley house has steam heat?
faq.a: The radiators and piping decide the job more than the nameplate on the old boiler. Steam systems depend on the right water level and piping, and a new boiler should be sized to the radiators as they are today. With 34.9% of units built in 1939 or earlier, steam is a fair question.

air-conditioning-installation-repair.quickAnswer: Wellesley has the oldest median home of the 50 towns (built 1954), and houses of that vintage often have no cooling plan. Ductless heads, high-velocity ducts or a carefully routed central system are the usual options, shaped by the layout and any historic limits.
body: ## Adding cooling to houses that were built without it

Air conditioning was not the norm when much of Wellesley was built, and a median build year of 1954 puts a large share of the housing in that period. Adding cooling means finding space for equipment nobody planned for. The climate is warm-summer humid continental, per Wikipedia, with high humidity and precipitation year-round, so taking moisture out of the air counts as much as lowering the temperature.
### Options for old construction

- **Ductless mini-splits:** an outdoor unit and a wall or ceiling head in each room or zone, with no ducts.
- **High-velocity systems:** small flexible ducts that fit through walls and attics without major demolition.
- **Conventional central air:** possible where there is space for large ducts, usually in newer houses or after a renovation.
### Historic constraints

Cottage Street and its alleys are designated a historic district, and most of the houses there date from around the 1860s. Equipment on the visible faces of protected buildings may be restricted. It makes sense to check with the historic commission early, since the location of an outdoor unit may need approval.
### Newer and rebuilt homes

Wellesley has 1,544 homes from 2000 on, 974 of them from 2010 or later. A newer or fully rebuilt house is often tight, ducted and zoned, with large windows and high ceilings. Cooling loads can be considerable. Careful duct design and zoning keep upstairs rooms comfortable. Sizing that ignores the windows and sun exposure can leave rooms uncomfortable.

### The value of getting it right
With a median home value of $1,424,400, the 2nd highest of the 50 towns, a cooling retrofit that cuts into a plaster ceiling or leaves the top floor warm is a costly mistake. Detached houses are 82.3% of units, so most jobs involve routing lines through a single-family house with its own attic or basement.
### Cooling from a heat pump

A heat pump cools as well as heats, so it can replace a failing air conditioner and handle part of the winter load. For rebate details specific to Wellesley's municipal electric utility, see the [heat pump page](/cities/wellesley/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).
### Repair or replace

A failed capacitor or dirty coil is usually a repair. When the compressor goes on a well-worn unit, replacing it is usually the better path. We give you the reasoning and the estimate in writing before starting.

faq.q: Can a Wellesley house with radiators get central air?
faq.a: Yes, through a new duct system, a high-velocity system or ductless units. The best option depends on attic and closet space, ceiling height and how much of the house needs cooling.

faq.q: Will an air conditioner be allowed on a historic house?
faq.a: It depends on where it goes and whether the house is in the historic district. Check with the historic commission before you order. Placement options may include less visible spots.

faq.q: Which is better for an old Wellesley house, ductless or high-velocity?
faq.a: Neither wins everywhere. Ductless heads need no ducts but put a unit in each room. High-velocity lines fit through walls and attics and hide the equipment, which suits finished rooms. Attic space, ceiling height and how many rooms need cooling usually decide it, and a site visit settles the rest.

heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits.quickAnswer: Wellesley's electricity comes from a municipal light plant, so the rebate depends on how the house heats. With 6,379 gas homes against 1,511 on oil and a median build year of 1954, the weatherization question comes first for most owners.
body: ## Heat pumps when the utility is municipal

Wikipedia notes that Wellesley is served by the Wellesley Municipal Light Plant. In a municipal-utility town, Mass Save's heat pump rebates generally cover only gas-heated homes with a Mass Save sponsor, and every other home looks to the Light Plant's own program. Where Mass Save does apply, the 2026 whole-home figure is $2,650 per ton up to $8,500 once the house is weatherized, and the rest is on our [main heat pump page](/services/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).
### Which homes fall on which side

Gas heats 6,379 Wellesley homes (71.2%), the 3rd-highest share of the 50 towns, so most owners sit on the gas side of that rule. The 1,511 homes on oil (16.9%), the 855 on electricity (9.5%) and the 127 on bottled gas (1.4%) sit on the other side. The oil group is the one with the clearest case for leaving deliveries behind.
### The age test in an old town

Just 1,544 homes (16.6%) date from 2000 or later, while 6,940 (74.5%) predate 1980, the 2nd-highest share in the 50 towns. In the oldest group, the 3,255 units from 1939 or earlier, an energy assessment is the likely first step, and air sealing and attic insulation may come before any equipment is sized.
### Partner, not replacement

A heat pump can work next to an existing gas system rather than replace it, and cooling is a common first reason to add one. Houses with good ductwork can take a ducted unit. Radiator-heated houses and additions usually suit ductless heads, and the historic district's protected buildings may favor equipment that keeps the exterior clean.
### Sizing after additions

A house that has had additions may carry a load different from the one on paper, so ask for the calculation behind any quote. See our [cooling page](/cities/wellesley/air-conditioning-installation-repair) for how heat pumps help in summer.

faq.q: I heat with oil in Wellesley. Is Mass Save available to me?
faq.a: Probably not directly, since the utility is municipal. Wellesley has 1,511 oil-heated homes, and their owners look to the Light Plant's own heat pump program. Ask the Light Plant what it offers and what it requires before you buy anything.

faq.q: I heat with gas. Does the Mass Save route apply to my house?
faq.a: Possibly, if your gas supplier is a Mass Save sponsor and the house passes the weatherization test. Gas is the main fuel for 71.2% of Wellesley homes, so this is the common case. Check masssave.com for current terms before you commit.

faq.q: Will a heat pump work in an old Wellesley house?
faq.a: It can, with a proper load calculation and some weatherization. Cold-climate models are designed for Massachusetts winters. With a median build year of 1954, many Wellesley houses will want an assessment first, and installation quality matters more than brand.

hvac-maintenance-tune-ups.quickAnswer: With the oldest median house of the 50 towns, older houses can have aging pipes, radiators and ducts. A yearly check catches problems early, and it matters most for oil burners and boilers that have outlived their expected life.
body: ## Looking after systems in old houses

A house that has stood since the early twentieth century may have seen several boilers. Maintenance keeps the current one honest and tells you what it has left. Gas heats most Wellesley homes, so gas boilers and furnaces are the most common systems to service, with a smaller group of oil burners.

### Why age drives the schedule
Wellesley has the oldest median home of the 50 towns (1954), and 34.9% of units date from 1939 or earlier. A house that old may have had several boilers, which is why a first visit is also a survey of what is actually installed, from the tank to the thermostat.
### Gas
On a gas system the visit looks at the burner, the heat exchanger and the vent. That is the quickest way to catch a cracked part or a blocked flue before it becomes a safety problem.
### Oil and bottled gas

Only 1,511 homes burn oil and 127 use bottled gas, so the ones that do deserve attention. Oil systems need an annual cleaning. We also look at the tank, the fill and vent lines and the filter, since an old tank is a risk in its own right.
### Steam and hot-water boilers

- Test the low-water cutoff and the pressure controls.
- Look for leaks at valves and joints.
- Bleed radiators that heat unevenly.
- Check the expansion tank on hot-water systems.
### Heat pumps and air conditioners

Coils, filters, drains and refrigerant-side checks in spring, before the first hot spell. Outdoor units need clearance from shrubs and snow. Check the municipal utility's heat pump program for any conditions.
### Rental owners
With 15.6% of households renting, a boiler that fails on a cold night is a tenant problem and a legal one. A check before October beats an emergency call.
### Signs to call early

- Short cycling or odd noises.
- Uneven rooms.
- A smell, soot or water around the equipment.
- A bill that jumps with no change in use.
See the [heating page](/cities/wellesley/heating-installation-repair) if a check shows the unit is at the end of its life.

faq.q: How often should a Wellesley boiler be serviced?
faq.a: Once a year, ideally in late summer or early fall. Older steam and hot-water boilers tend to benefit most because wear can show up first in safety controls, valves and burners.
It depends on the equipment and what the visit covers. Ask for a written estimate that lists what the visit covers, and compare it against the system's age and condition.

faq.q: When should an oil system in Wellesley be cleaned?
faq.a: Before the heating season starts, which in practice means late summer or early fall. Oil heats 16.9% of Wellesley homes, well under the 36.5% of the middle town, so an oil owner here is in the minority and should not assume the neighbors' routine applies.

indoor-air-quality.quickAnswer: More than a third of Wellesley's housing units were built in 1939 or earlier, while others are newer and tighter. Dust, damp basements and ventilation are the usual concerns.
body: ## Air in a town of old houses and new rebuilds
Wellesley's housing runs from the earliest construction to houses finished in the last decade, and air quality differs along that range. Older ones tend to leak, and new ones tend to be tight.

### Counting the old and the new
The oldest group is large: 3,255 units (34.9%) date from 1939 or earlier, and another 2,251 (24.2%) from 1940 to 1959. At the other end 974 units (10.5%) were built since 2010. The air problems of those two groups are close to opposites: one leaks, the other holds on to what is inside, and the right fixes differ as well.
### Old houses

Plaster walls, old foundations and wood framing tend to hold dust and moisture. Gaps let in outdoor air, which dilutes some pollutants but brings in pollen and damp. Old ducts, where they exist, can hold years of dust. Where a renovation would disturb old paint or insulation, a specialist should test first.
### Tight and rebuilt houses

The Massachusetts Stretch Building Code, adopted in Wellesley effective January 2012, can push new construction toward tighter, more energy-efficient houses. In a tight house moisture and cooking fumes have nowhere to go unless ventilation moves them. Bath fans and range hoods that vent outdoors, and sometimes an ERV or HRV, are standard fixes.
### Humidity

Basements in old houses often smell musty in summer. A dehumidifier treats the symptom; a leak or a failed drain tile needs repair where it starts. In winter heated air gets dry, and a humidifier tied to the system can help if the house feels uncomfortable.
### Filters
A better filter is a cheap improvement if the blower can handle it. In older ducted systems, we check airflow first. Swapping filters on time counts as much as the rating.
### Renovation dust

A remodel can leave construction dust that clogs filters and coat ducts. Seal returns and registers during work and replace filters when it is done. If dust got in the ducts, cleaning may be warranted.
### Testing

One reading of humidity, carbon monoxide or particles is a single moment. We use it to hunt for the source. Our [heat pump page](/cities/wellesley/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits) covers equipment that also dehumidifies.

faq.q: Do old houses have worse air quality?
faq.a: Not necessarily, but the issues differ. Leaks, dust, damp basements and old materials are typical. Tight new houses have different problems: moisture and not enough fresh air.

faq.q: Should I clean my ducts after a renovation?
faq.a: Often it makes sense, especially if the system ran during demolition or sanding. An inspection comes first, and it shows whether cleaning would make a difference.

faq.q: Does a Wellesley house built since 2010 need mechanical ventilation?
faq.a: Often it benefits from it. A house built since 2010 is likely tight, and Wellesley has 974 such units. Working bath fans and a range hood that vents outdoors come first, and an ERV or HRV is the next step when humidity or stale air persists.
